body.text: Sydney to lead Australia's housing price recovery, analysis predicts
In short:
House prices are predicted to fall between 10 and 13 per cent by mid-2027, according to new data.
In its forecast report, Domain says Sydney house prices will then rebound stronger than any other capital city.
According to the forecast, median prices are expected to increase from $1.6 million to $1.7 million over the 12 months to December 2027.
Australia's housing market downturn is set to drag on in every major city into next year, but new analysis suggests Sydney will bounce back and lead a national price recovery.
Domain's forecast report, released today, predicts house prices will fall between 10 and 13 per cent across major capital cities by mid-2027, driven by high borrowing costs and weak buyer confidence.
In Sydney, house prices are expected to drop by 10 per cent by June 2027 before stabilising in the second half of the year.
The report predicts Sydney, Brisbane and Perth to record the sharpest housing downturn but expects Sydney to have the strongest price rebound of any capital city.
David Cannington, a senior residential economist at Domain, said buyer confidence had placed downward pressure on the market.
"Home buyer confidence has been impacted by higher interest rates, elevated inflation and then on top of that, the changes to housing investment tax policy earlier in the year," he told the ABC.
Mr Cannington said buyers and sellers were already adjusting to the changes in market conditions, with 2027 shaping up to be a "year of transition".
"We expect price falls to be softer in 2027 than they were this year and by the second half of next year we expect the market will be finding its footing," he said.
Market lull a 'double-edged sword'
Sales executive Daniel Eid from Laing+Simmons said he was seeing price guides for homes change almost every week.
"There's not much movement at all; properties are sitting on the market," he said.
"Anyone that's in a situation where they need to sell, they have to drop their prices all the way down. So it's actually negatively impacted on our vendors that we're dealing with."
He said despite property prices dropping, high interest rates meant banks were being stricter with lending.
"I do believe that there are a lot of buyers that are actually saying that they're holding off till next year, forecasting that the market's going to continue to drop.
"I think it's kind of been a double-edged sword … the prices may come back up but you know it's very hard to predict."
Sharp rise in distressed sales listings
The downturn in Australia's housing prices is occurring alongside a rise in the number of distressed sale listings.
A distressed sale is when a property is sold quickly, often at a loss, and typically occurs when an owner is under financial hardship.
According to SQM Research, distressed sale listings surpassed 300,000 in October, the highest level in five years.
In NSW, the number of distressed sales listings has jumped from 870 to 1,190 — about one third — since January.
SQM managing director Louis Christopher said distressed listings had risen the fastest in the past two to three months and more quickly compared to 2022, a trend that was concerning.
"When they climb this fast it tells us more households and investors are under financial pressure and being forced to sell," he said.
"It also usually comes before additional weaker prices."
Mr Christopher said that while more housing stock was coming onto the market, properties were taking longer to sell.
"That's the setting where forced sales start to really build," he said.

Mr Christopher said the upswing could be a precursor of a broader shift in market conditions, however distressed listings were still lower than the 2024 peak of 1,400 and well below the levels seen in 2020.
Interest yet to completely wane
McGrath sales agent Aaron Lih said in recent months he had received calls from clients inquiring about selling.
He said some owners were wanting to sell due to interest rates becoming too expensive while others wanted to seek opportunity elsewhere in the market.
"A lot of owners that we appraised months ago or last year are reaching out to us now," he said.
"We have to say to them, that price that we told you nine or 12 months ago, is probably $50,000, $100,000 or $200,000 less than what it is today."
Mr Lih anticipated the state election in March would affect buyer confidence, but expected the market to pick up in six months.
He said in the meantime, he was still seeing interest from first home buyers and families wanting to upsize.
"If you have the capacity to buy, I think it's a great time to buy, this is the market,"
"When the market's hot, everyone's asking for a slow market. All the buyers are saying, 'Ah, the market is too hot, it's too crazy,' and they want it to slow down.
"This is what everyone's been asking for."
